Archive item 1: Habitat Mapping Report: Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve
Source format: habitat mapping report

2.2 Vegetation Classification
Vegetation types were classified using the revised Champion and Seth (1968) classification, adapted for the Western Ghats by the Kerala Forest Research Institute (KFRI). Classification criteria included dominant tree species, canopy height, leaf phenology, and the presence of indicator species. Satellite imagery from Sentinel-2 (10m resolution) and Landsat-8 (30m resolution) were used for preliminary vegetation mapping, followed by ground verification of all classified polygons.

2.3 Zone Boundary Delineation
Habitat zone boundaries were delineated based on vegetation type transitions, altitude, and known wildlife movement patterns. GPS coordinates were recorded for all boundary points, and boundaries were subsequently digitized in GIS. The boundaries presented in this report supersede the preliminary boundaries presented in the 2020 reconnaissance report (WTI/RD/PR/NBR/2020-03), which were based on limited ground-truthing.

3. VEGETATION TYPES IDENTIFIED

The 2021 survey identified the following major vegetation types within the Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve:

3.1 Tropical Wet Evergreen Forest
This vegetation type is characterized by multi-layered canopy structure, with trees reaching heights of 35-45 meters. The canopy is dense and closed, with a high diversity of tree species. Characteristic species include Cullenia exarillata, Palaquium ellipticum, Mesua ferrea, and Hopea parviflora. The understory comprises dense shrub and herb layers, with abundant epiphytes and lianas. This forest type occurs in areas receiving high annual rainfall exceeding 2000 mm, typically at altitudes between 900 and 1500 meters.

3.4 Tropical Dry Thorn Forest
This vegetation type occurs in the driest portions of the reserve, typically at altitudes below 300 meters in the rain shadow areas of the Eastern Ghats extension. Characteristic species include Acacia chundra, Prosopis juliflora, and Ziziphus mauritiana. The canopy is open and low, with trees reaching heights of only 6-10 meters. This forest type receives annual rainfall below 800 mm and experiences a prolonged dry season of 6-8 months.

3.5 Montane Shola-Grassland Mosaic
This vegetation type occurs at altitudes above 1500 meters, characterized by a mosaic of stunted evergreen forest patches (sholas) interspersed with grasslands. Shola species include Ilex wightiana, Rhododendron arboreum, and Michelia nilagirica. The grasslands are dominated by species of Chrysopogon, Themeda, and Arundinella. This vegetation type is of particular importance for the endemic Nilgiri tahr and several species of birds.

3.6 Plantations and Secondary Scrub
This category includes teak, eucalyptus, and wattle plantations, as well as secondary scrub regrowth in areas previously cleared for agriculture or timber extraction. These areas are included in the habitat map but are not classified as natural vegetation types.

4. HABITAT ZONE DELINEATION

The Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve has_habitat_zone tropical wet evergreen forest, as recorded in the habitat mapping report. Record status: current. This zone is the largest contiguous habitat zone within the reserve, covering approximately 2,850 square kilometers. The zone boundaries were delineated based on the presence of characteristic evergreen forest species and the altitudinal range described in Section 3.1.

4.1 Zone 1: Tropical Wet Evergreen Forest Zone
This zone extends across the western and southwestern portions of the reserve, including the Silent Valley National Park, parts of the Attappadi Reserve Forest, and the New Amarambalam Reserved Forest. The zone boundary begins at coordinate 11.2138°N, 76.5412°E near the western edge of the reserve and extends eastward to coordinate 11.3127°N, 76.8894°E, following the contour line at approximately 900 meters altitude. The southern boundary of this zone runs along the Palghat Gap area, while the northern boundary extends into the Wayanad region. The zone is characterized by high species diversity, with an average of 320 tree species per hectare recorded in the sampling plots.

4.
**4.2 Zone 2: Moist Deciduous Forest Zone**

This zone forms a broad transitional belt between the wet evergreen zone and the drier areas to the east and south. It occupies the mid-elevation slopes, generally between 600 and 1100 meters, and is best developed in the Bandipur, Nagarhole, and Mudumalai Tiger Reserve areas, extending into the Sigur Plateau and the foothills of the Wayanad region. The zone boundary begins near the eastern edge of Zone 1 at coordinate 11.3127°N, 76.8894°E and extends northeastward, following the 900-meter contour until it grades into the dry deciduous zone below 600 meters. The southern limit of this zone is marked by the Moyar River valley, while the northern extent reaches into the Kabini Reservoir catchment.

The vegetation in this zone is characterized by a mix of deciduous species, with a canopy height averaging 20-28 meters. Dominant tree species include Terminalia elliptica, Tectona grandis, Dalbergia latifolia, Pterocarpus marsupium, and Lagerstroemia lanceolata. The understorey is typically composed of Helicteres isora, Grewia tiliifolia, and Ziziphus oenoplia. In areas with shallower soils or on rocky outcrops, the forest opens up into scrubby patches dominated by Lantana camara and Chromolaena odorata, both of which are invasive and have been expanding in recent years. Bamboo brakes of Bambusa arundinacea and Dendrocalamus strictus are common along drainage lines and in areas that have been subjected to historical clearing or fire.

Sampling plots in this zone recorded an average of 145 tree species per hectare, a figure that is significantly lower than the evergreen zone but still high for deciduous forests in the Western Ghats. The zone supports a substantial population of large herbivores, including Asian elephant (Elephas maximus), gaur (Bos gaurus), chital (Axis axis), and sambar (Rusa unicolor). Carnivore presence is confirmed through scat and camera trap records for tiger (Panthera tigris), leopard (Panthera pardus), and dhole (Cuon alpinus). The Moyar River corridor within this zone is a critical elephant migratory route, and seasonal water holes in the Sigur Plateau are heavily used during the dry months of March to May.

**4.3 Zone 3: Dry Deciduous and Thorn Scrub Zone**

This zone occupies the eastern and southeastern portions of the reserve, at elevations below 600 meters. It is best represented in the eastern parts of Mudumalai, the Sathyamangalam Tiger Reserve, and the drier tracts of the Biligiriranganatha Swamy Temple (BRT) Tiger Reserve. The zone experiences a prolonged dry season of 6-8 months, with annual rainfall typically between 500 and 900 millimeters, most of which falls during the northeast monsoon (October to December). The zone boundary runs along the Moyar River in the west, extends eastward past the Hasanur plateau, and continues into the drier foothills of the Eastern Ghats transition.

The vegetation is a mosaic of dry deciduous forest, thorn scrub, and savanna woodland. Characteristic tree species include Anogeissus latifolia, Chloroxylon swietenia, Acacia chundra, Hardwickia binata, and Albizia amara. In the thorn scrub patches, species of Acacia, Ziziphus, and Capparis are dominant, often forming impenetrable thickets. The ground layer is sparse, with grasses such as Heteropogon contortus, Cenchrus ciliaris, and Aristida setacea. This zone is particularly important for the endangered yellow-throated bulbul (Pycnonotus xantholaemus), which is restricted to rocky scrub habitats in this region, and for the Indian pangolin (Manis crassicaudata), which is recorded from burrow and track evidence.

The dry zone is subject to frequent anthropogenic pressure, including livestock grazing, fire, and fuelwood collection. During the survey period, 34% of the sampling plots in this zone showed signs of recent fire, and 41% had evidence of livestock dung. This zone is not a primary habitat for the endemic Nilgiri tahr, which is confined to the montane grasslands of Zone 4, but it does provide habitat for a distinct set of dry-zone specialists.

documents.title: Habitat Mapping Report: Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve
documents.content:
2.2 Vegetation Classification
Vegetation types were classified using the revised Champion and Seth (1968) classification, adapted for the Western Ghats by the Kerala Forest Research Institute (KFRI). Classification criteria included dominant tree species, canopy height, leaf phenology, and the presence of indicator species. Satellite imagery from Sentinel-2 (10m resolution) and Landsat-8 (30m resolution) were used for preliminary vegetation mapping, followed by ground verification of all classified polygons.

2.3 Zone Boundary Delineation
Habitat zone boundaries were delineated based on vegetation type transitions, altitude, and known wildlife movement patterns. GPS coordinates were recorded for all boundary points, and boundaries were subsequently digitized in GIS. The boundaries presented in this report supersede the preliminary boundaries presented in the 2020 reconnaissance report (WTI/RD/PR/NBR/2020-03), which were based on limited ground-truthing.

3. VEGETATION TYPES IDENTIFIED

The 2021 survey identified the following major vegetation types within the Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve:

3.1 Tropical Wet Evergreen Forest
This vegetation type is characterized by multi-layered canopy structure, with trees reaching heights of 35-45 meters. The canopy is dense and closed, with a high diversity of tree species. Characteristic species include Cullenia exarillata, Palaquium ellipticum, Mesua ferrea, and Hopea parviflora. The understory comprises dense shrub and herb layers, with abundant epiphytes and lianas. This forest type occurs in areas receiving high annual rainfall exceeding 2000 mm, typically at altitudes between 900 and 1500 meters.

3.4 Tropical Dry Thorn Forest
This vegetation type occurs in the driest portions of the reserve, typically at altitudes below 300 meters in the rain shadow areas of the Eastern Ghats extension. Characteristic species include Acacia chundra, Prosopis juliflora, and Ziziphus mauritiana. The canopy is open and low, with trees reaching heights of only 6-10 meters. This forest type receives annual rainfall below 800 mm and experiences a prolonged dry season of 6-8 months.

3.5 Montane Shola-Grassland Mosaic
This vegetation type occurs at altitudes above 1500 meters, characterized by a mosaic of stunted evergreen forest patches (sholas) interspersed with grasslands. Shola species include Ilex wightiana, Rhododendron arboreum, and Michelia nilagirica. The grasslands are dominated by species of Chrysopogon, Themeda, and Arundinella. This vegetation type is of particular importance for the endemic Nilgiri tahr and several species of birds.

3.6 Plantations and Secondary Scrub
This category includes teak, eucalyptus, and wattle plantations, as well as secondary scrub regrowth in areas previously cleared for agriculture or timber extraction. These areas are included in the habitat map but are not classified as natural vegetation types.

4. HABITAT ZONE DELINEATION

The Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve has_habitat_zone tropical wet evergreen forest, as recorded in the habitat mapping report. Record status: current. This zone is the largest contiguous habitat zone within the reserve, covering approximately 2,850 square kilometers. The zone boundaries were delineated based on the presence of characteristic evergreen forest species and the altitudinal range described in Section 3.1.

4.1 Zone 1: Tropical Wet Evergreen Forest Zone
This zone extends across the western and southwestern portions of the reserve, including the Silent Valley National Park, parts of the Attappadi Reserve Forest, and the New Amarambalam Reserved Forest. The zone boundary begins at coordinate 11.2138°N, 76.5412°E near the western edge of the reserve and extends eastward to coordinate 11.3127°N, 76.8894°E, following the contour line at approximately 900 meters altitude. The southern boundary of this zone runs along the Palghat Gap area, while the northern boundary extends into the Wayanad region. The zone is characterized by high species diversity, with an average of 320 tree species per hectare recorded in the sampling plots.

documents.title: Habitat Mapping Report: Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve
documents.content:
**4.2 Zone 2: Moist Deciduous Forest Zone**

This zone forms a broad transitional belt between the wet evergreen zone and the drier areas to the east and south. It occupies the mid-elevation slopes, generally between 600 and 1100 meters, and is best developed in the Bandipur, Nagarhole, and Mudumalai Tiger Reserve areas, extending into the Sigur Plateau and the foothills of the Wayanad region. The zone boundary begins near the eastern edge of Zone 1 at coordinate 11.3127°N, 76.8894°E and extends northeastward, following the 900-meter contour until it grades into the dry deciduous zone below 600 meters. The southern limit of this zone is marked by the Moyar River valley, while the northern extent reaches into the Kabini Reservoir catchment.

The vegetation in this zone is characterized by a mix of deciduous species, with a canopy height averaging 20-28 meters. Dominant tree species include Terminalia elliptica, Tectona grandis, Dalbergia latifolia, Pterocarpus marsupium, and Lagerstroemia lanceolata. The understorey is typically composed of Helicteres isora, Grewia tiliifolia, and Ziziphus oenoplia. In areas with shallower soils or on rocky outcrops, the forest opens up into scrubby patches dominated by Lantana camara and Chromolaena odorata, both of which are invasive and have been expanding in recent years. Bamboo brakes of Bambusa arundinacea and Dendrocalamus strictus are common along drainage lines and in areas that have been subjected to historical clearing or fire.

Sampling plots in this zone recorded an average of 145 tree species per hectare, a figure that is significantly lower than the evergreen zone but still high for deciduous forests in the Western Ghats. The zone supports a substantial population of large herbivores, including Asian elephant (Elephas maximus), gaur (Bos gaurus), chital (Axis axis), and sambar (Rusa unicolor). Carnivore presence is confirmed through scat and camera trap records for tiger (Panthera tigris), leopard (Panthera pardus), and dhole (Cuon alpinus). The Moyar River corridor within this zone is a critical elephant migratory route, and seasonal water holes in the Sigur Plateau are heavily used during the dry months of March to May.

**4.3 Zone 3: Dry Deciduous and Thorn Scrub Zone**

This zone occupies the eastern and southeastern portions of the reserve, at elevations below 600 meters. It is best represented in the eastern parts of Mudumalai, the Sathyamangalam Tiger Reserve, and the drier tracts of the Biligiriranganatha Swamy Temple (BRT) Tiger Reserve. The zone experiences a prolonged dry season of 6-8 months, with annual rainfall typically between 500 and 900 millimeters, most of which falls during the northeast monsoon (October to December). The zone boundary runs along the Moyar River in the west, extends eastward past the Hasanur plateau, and continues into the drier foothills of the Eastern Ghats transition.

The vegetation is a mosaic of dry deciduous forest, thorn scrub, and savanna woodland. Characteristic tree species include Anogeissus latifolia, Chloroxylon swietenia, Acacia chundra, Hardwickia binata, and Albizia amara. In the thorn scrub patches, species of Acacia, Ziziphus, and Capparis are dominant, often forming impenetrable thickets. The ground layer is sparse, with grasses such as Heteropogon contortus, Cenchrus ciliaris, and Aristida setacea. This zone is particularly important for the endangered yellow-throated bulbul (Pycnonotus xantholaemus), which is restricted to rocky scrub habitats in this region, and for the Indian pangolin (Manis crassicaudata), which is recorded from burrow and track evidence.

The dry zone is subject to frequent anthropogenic pressure, including livestock grazing, fire, and fuelwood collection. During the survey period, 34% of the sampling plots in this zone showed signs of recent fire, and 41% had evidence of livestock dung. This zone is not a primary habitat for the endemic Nilgiri tahr, which is confined to the montane grasslands of Zone 4, but it does provide habitat for a distinct set of dry-zone specialists.
